title: VGSH vs. SMB: A Comparison of Two Top Short-Term Bond ETFs
author: John Ballard
description: Vanguard's VGSH and VanEck's SMB are compared as short-term bond ETF options. VGSH offers lower costs (0.03% expense ratio), higher yields (3.85%), and larger assets ($33.9B), making it attractive for general investors. SMB provides tax-exempt municipal bond income (2.76% yield) suited for high-bracket taxpayers, though with slightly higher expenses (0.07%) and lower liquidity ($312.7M). Both funds minimize interest rate risk through short durations, with VGSH having ~2 years maturity versus SMB's 3+ years.

insights.sentiment_reasoning: VGSH is presented favorably with the lowest expense ratio (0.03%), highest dividend yield (3.85%), significantly larger asset base ($33.9B), and lower volatility (beta 0.23). These factors make it the more cost-effective and liquid choice for most investors.

SMB is presented as a viable alternative with specific advantages (tax-exempt income, ESG screening) suited for high-tax-bracket investors, but with drawbacks including higher expense ratio (0.07%), lower yield (2.76%), smaller asset base ($312.7M), and greater interest rate sensitivity. It's positioned as a specialized option rather than a superior choice.

title: Vanguard's VGSH or BSV: Which Short-Term Bond ETF Belongs in Your Portfolio Today?
author: Sara Appino
description: Vanguard offers two short-term bond ETFs with identical 0.03% expense ratios but different risk profiles. VGSH focuses exclusively on U.S. Treasury securities for maximum safety with lower volatility, while BSV includes investment-grade corporate bonds and international debt for higher yields but greater drawdown risk. The choice depends on investor risk tolerance and desired credit exposure.

insights.sentiment_reasoning: Highlighted as the more defensive choice with the lowest credit risk, smallest maximum drawdown (5.6%), and pure government-backed safety. Ideal for conservative investors seeking cash-like behavior in their bond allocation.

Presented as an attractive option for investors seeking broader diversification and higher yield (4.0% vs 3.8%), with slightly stronger 1-year returns (3.3% vs 3.1%). Suitable for those comfortable with modest corporate credit risk.

title: Treasury ETFs: VGSH Holds Size Edge Over SCHO
author: Jake Lerch
description: Vanguard Short-Term Treasury ETF (VGSH) and Schwab Short-Term U.S. Treasury ETF (SCHO) are nearly identical Treasury bond ETFs with matching 0.03% expense ratios, 4.0% yields, and -0.2% one-year returns. The main difference is VGSH's larger asset base of $32.7 billion versus SCHO's $11.9 billion, giving VGSH a slight liquidity advantage for investors.

insights.sentiment_reasoning: VGSH is positioned favorably due to its significantly larger AUM ($32.7B vs $11.9B), which provides better liquidity and easier trading for investors. The article explicitly recommends VGSH with 'a very slight edge' over its competitor.

SCHO is presented as a viable alternative with identical costs, yields, and performance metrics to VGSH. While it's a solid option, it is disadvantaged only by its smaller AUM, which slightly impacts trading liquidity. The article notes it as equally suitable for investors.

title: 3 Vanguard ETFs to Buy to Protect Your Portfolio From a Potential Stock Market Crash
author: David Dierking
description: After three years of strong S&P 500 gains, investors are considering portfolio protection strategies. The article recommends three Vanguard ETFs: VGSH (short-term Treasury bonds) for low volatility, BND (total bond market) for diversified bond exposure, and VFMV (minimum volatility stocks) for defensive equity positioning. These options offer varying levels of downside protection in case of a market correction.

Recommended for diversified bond exposure across Treasuries, MBS, and corporate bonds with a 4.2% yield and controlled volatility.

title: BSV Offers Broader Bond Exposure Than VGSH
author: John Ballard
description: Vanguard's Short-Term Bond ETF (BSV) and Short-Term Treasury ETF (VGSH) both offer ultra-low 0.03% expense ratios, but differ in composition. BSV provides broader exposure with 3,115 holdings across government, corporate, and international bonds with $68.2B in AUM, while VGSH focuses exclusively on U.S. Treasuries with 92 holdings and $30.4B in AUM. VGSH slightly outperformed over 5 years with higher dividend yield, but BSV showed stronger 1-year returns. The choice depends on investor preference for safety (VGSH) versus broader diversification (BSV).

insights.sentiment_reasoning: BSV is highlighted for its broader bond exposure across government, corporate, and international investment-grade bonds, larger AUM of $68.2B, higher 1-year return of 5.9%, and steadily trending higher yield. These factors position it favorably for investors seeking diversified fixed-income exposure.

VGSH is presented positively for its exclusive focus on U.S. Treasuries providing maximum credit safety, slightly higher 5-year returns, higher dividend yield of 3.96%, and lower maximum drawdown of 5.70%. It appeals to conservative investors seeking stability and safety.
